title: The Name Collector
summary: At a fair that only appears when it snows, an old man buys names in exchange for warm coins. Bento sells his as a joke — and discovers that without a name, no one can call him home anymore.

chapters.title: The Velvet Stall
chapters.body:
The winter fair of Thornbrook had a rule no one could explain, but everyone respected: it only opened when it snowed, and closed the moment the last flake touched the ground. That was why the village children learned to pray for snow the way other children pray for sun.

Bento was eleven years old and had a collection of useless things he was deeply proud of: a jay's feather, a brass button, three stones he swore were dragon eggs yet to hatch. He loved the fair because the fair was made of people like him — people who valued what others threw away.

That night it snowed lightly, a playful snow, and Bento ran between the stalls with his coat half-buttoned. There was a man selling shadows already folded, ready to wear. There was a woman who traded bad memories for secondhand ones, promising that the used ones hurt less. And, at the very end, leaning against the old wall where the fair always finished, there was a stall Bento had never seen.

It was lined with wine-colored velvet, worn at the corners, and it smelled of baked apple and of something older underneath, like the smell of a book no one has opened in a long time. Behind the counter stood a thin old man in a frock coat, with long fingers and a smile that reached his eyes a little too late, as if he had to remember to smile.

"Come in, come in," he said. "You have the look of a collector."

Bento went in because it was true, and because the stall was warm in a good way, and because at his age an invitation still weighed more than a warning.

The old man sold neither shadows nor memories. On the shelves, in corked little glass vials, were what looked like wisps of light — each a slightly different color, each moving slowly, as if breathing.

"What are they?" Bento asked.

"Names," said the old man, and took a vial from the shelf, turning it against the lamp. Inside, the little light glowed an amber shade. "This one belonged to a boy named Terence. He sold it to me some forty winters ago. Said he thought the name too ugly. Traded it for a warm coin and went off happy, whistling."

"And what happened to him?"

The old man set the vial back on the shelf very carefully, like someone returning a bird to its nest.

"Ah, that," he said, "is precisely the part the customers never ask before. Only after."

Bento should have found that strange. He should have noticed that the old man hadn't answered the question, only nudged it along like someone kicking a can down the street. But he was eleven years old, and a warm coin gleaming in the old man's palm seemed, in that instant, the most interesting thing in the whole world.

"Is the coin real?" he asked.

"More real than most things," said the old man. "Stays warm in your pocket all night. Never cools. Never vanishes." He leaned over the counter, and the velvet behind him seemed to darken a shade. "It costs only one thing, and it's a thing you don't even use properly. A name. Yours, for instance. Bento is a fine name, but what does it do for you, eh? You don't call yourself by it. Others do the calling. Why give away for free to others what could be worth a coin that never cools?"

And that, Bento would understand much later, was the oldest trick in the world: to make a person believe that the thing most their own was, in fact, the least important.

chapters.title: The Coin That Doesn't Cool
chapters.body:
Bento sold his name.

Not all at once — the old man was far too patient for haste. First he let the boy hold the coin, feel the warmth rising through his fingers on a snowy night. Then he let him imagine everything a magic coin could buy. And when Bento said, half laughing, half doubting, "fine, you can keep it," the old man simply nodded, as if they were trading a playing card.

"Say your name one last time," the old man asked, uncorking an empty vial. "Loud and clear. Names are shy; they need to be called to come out."

"Bento," said Bento.

The word came out of his mouth as it always had. But this time it didn't come back. It was like blowing out a candle: there was the breath, and then the dark where the flame had been. A pale little light, honey-colored, floated from the boy's mouth and coiled inside the vial. The old man corked it quickly. The light beat against the glass once, twice, like a moth, and then went still.

"There," said the old man, setting the vial on the shelf, between Terence and a girl named Aurelia. "Done and done."

The coin was warm indeed. Bento squeezed it in his pocket and went out into the snow smiling, feeling like the cleverest boy in Thornbrook. The fair was already packing up — the last flakes were falling — and he ran home to show off his treasure.

It was at his own front door that the first strange thing happened.

He knocked. His mother opened it, drying her hands on her apron, and looked at him with a face Bento had never seen: not angry, not worried. Polite. The face you make for a distant neighbor.

"Yes, dear?" she said. "Are you looking for someone?"

"Mom, it's me," said Bento, and laughed, because it could only be a joke.

His mother frowned. Something passed through her eyes, a shadow of distress, like when we try to remember a dream and it slips away. She looked at the boy in the snow and felt — you could see that she felt — that she ought to know him, that there was a hole in his exact shape somewhere inside her chest. But the name that filled that hole had gone away inside a vial, and without the name she couldn't reach the rest.

"Are you lost, child?" she asked, and the word "child" hurt them both, because she said it the way you'd say it to any stranger's kid on the street. "Do you want to come in and warm up? It's such a cold night."

Bento did not go in. He ran off, and the warm coin in his pocket suddenly felt like the coldest thing he'd ever touched.

He spent the night huddled on the church steps. And he learned, hour by hour, what the old man hadn't explained. Without a name, he didn't disappear — everyone saw him. But no one held him in memory. People talked with him and, on turning the corner, forgot. The baker gave him a loaf out of pity and, a minute later, greeted him again like a stranger. It was like being a drop of water on a windowpane: present, glinting, and sliding out of everyone's memory before leaving a mark.

A name, he discovered, is not the label we wear. It is the handle by which the people who love us can pull us back when we get lost. And he had sold his for a coin that, however warm, did not know the way home.

chapters.title: The Price of Coming Back
chapters.body:
Bento waited for the snow.

It took nine days — nine days sleeping on doorsteps, eating what people gave him and then forgot they'd given, watching his own mother pass him on the street with a kind and distant nod. Nine days holding the warm coin and understanding, ever more deeply, that he had made the worst bargain in the history of Thornbrook.

On the ninth day, the sky turned the color of lead and the snow began. Bento ran for the old wall before the first flake even touched the ground. The fair was setting up, the stalls sprouting from the dark like mushrooms. And there, against the wall, the wine-colored velvet stall.

The old man didn't seem surprised.

"Ah," he said. "The customer who asks the questions after. They always come back. It's the saddest part of the trade, you know. I prefer the ones who never return. Terence never returned." He shrugged. "But you want your name back."

"I do," said Bento. "I'll give the coin back. Here." And he held out his hand with the warm coin on his palm.

The old man looked at the coin and laughed — not with malice, but with the weariness of someone who has heard the same offer a thousand times.

"It doesn't work that way, boy. The coin isn't the price of the name. The coin is the bait. You gave me the name for free, really; the coin was just so you'd think you'd gained something." He leaned in. "To buy a name back, the price is always higher than what was received for it. That's how the stall turns a profit. You gave me one name. To have it back, you must give me two."

"But I only have one," said Bento. "And you have it."

"Precisely," the old man smiled. "So give me someone else's name. Anyone will do. Tell me the name of someone you love, loud and clear, and I'll take it from them and put it in a vial, and give yours back. They'll end up like you are now: present, but loose in the world, forgotten by all. And you go home. Your mother will hug you at the door and cry with relief without knowing why she cried." He uncorked an empty vial and set it on the counter, between the two of them, waiting. "It's a fair price. You just pass along what was done to you. Most pay. It's astonishing how most pay."

And here was the real trap, the one the coin had only opened: it wasn't enough that Bento had been foolish. Now they were offering him the chance to be cruel, and calling it a repair.

Bento looked at the empty vial. He thought of his mother opening the door. He thought of saying her name — just two syllables, so easy — and going back to the warmth, to his bed, to being remembered. And he thought of her afterward, in the snow, knocking on doors that would close politely, becoming a drop on a windowpane.

"No," he said.

The old man raised an eyebrow.

"No? You'd rather stay like this? Forgotten forever?"

"I'd rather be forgotten than make someone else be," said Bento. And his voice trembled, but he did not take it back. "You said most pay. I'm not going to be most."

And then something happened that the old man, in all his winters, perhaps no longer expected. The honey-colored light, in the vial between Terence and Aurelia, began to beat hard. Because a name, at bottom, is the handle by which love pulls us back — and Bento, by refusing to steal someone else's love, had just proven that his name was still truly his, bought back with the one coin the stall couldn't counterfeit: a generous choice at an hour when the mean one was easier.

The vial burst. Not with a crash — with a light tinkle, like a small bell. The honey-colored light flew across the stall and coiled into Bento's chest, and he felt, all at once, his own name return into him like warmth returning to a numb finger.

"Bento," he said, and this time the word came back.

The old man recoiled. The velvet behind him looked more worn now, and the smell of baked apple had gone, leaving only the smell of the closed book underneath.

"Go," said the old man, and for the first time the smile didn't reach his eyes at all. "Before the snow stops."

Bento dropped the warm coin on the counter. It cooled at once, became an ordinary coin, dull and plain.

"Keep it," he said. "I thought it was worth something."

And he ran off through the snow, toward home, where his mother would open the door and fall to her knees and hug him crying without knowing why — knowing only that a hole in his exact shape had, at last, been filled again.

They say the velvet stall never appeared in Thornbrook again. But winter fairs exist everywhere, and snow falls on many villages, and somewhere, right now, an old man with long fingers is holding out a warm coin to a child who collects things — and explaining, very carefully, that a name is the least important thing in the world.
